aligned_passages.text: ### 9.4 A classical optimization algorithm The scalar Gaussian construction is not itself an algorithm on the matrix of SK couplings. A finite-disorder algorithm is obtained by importing the theorem of El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke. In their cited preprint, Assumption 2 asks for a strictly increasing minimizer of the zero-temperature Parisi functional on $\mathcal U$. The support theorem gives this property, and the imported attainment argument supplies the minimizer. Their Corollary 2.2 then returns, for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a randomized spin configuration within $\varepsilon n$ of the finite-instance maximum with probability tending to one. Its operation count is the one in the displayed Theorem 3 on p. 7; the preprint's running references call that result “Theorem 3.2.” [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, arXiv:2001.00904v1, pp. 7–8][eams20]. ### 5.1 The scalar value The support identities give a scalar representation of $P_*$. Set $M_t=u(t,X_t)$, the bounded gradient martingale satisfying $dM_t=a(t,X_t)\,dB_t$. The quadratic variations distinguish the two Hessian moments: $$ d\langle M\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)^2\,dt, \qquad d\langle M,B\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ Full support gives $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$, hence each increment $M_t-M_s$ has unconditional variance $t-s$. This normalises the discrete increments below. The first moment of $a$ instead gives covariance with the driving noise. Let $U$ be the almost-sure and $L^2$ limit of $M_t$. The value identity is $$ P_*=\mathbb E[UB_1] =\int_0^1\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt. \tag{10} $$ Boundedness gives $|U|\leq1$, while $\mathbb E M_t^2\to1$ gives $\mathbb E U^2=1$; therefore $U^2=1$ almost surely. To see the cancellation behind (10), the terminal convergence of the convex value functions gives $UX_1=|X_1|$, while Itô's formula gives $\mathcal P(\gamma)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt$. Multiplying $X_1=B_1+\int_0^1\gamma(t)M_t\,dt$ by $U$ cancels that integral because $\mathbb E[UM_t]=t$. The Parisi formula then gives (10). The endpoint limits and stochastic-integral covariance are proved in [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.1][FS] and the long record, [§6, “Recovering the value from a martingale”](../long/reasoning-record.md#scalar-value-identities). This argument uses full support, not the density corollary. In particular, convexity and Cauchy–Schwarz give $0\leq\mathbb E a\leq1$, so $$ 0\leq P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt\leq1-T. $$ One can therefore fix the terminal cutoff before discretising the diffusion. The gradient-martingale and value methods have antecedents in [Montanari, preprint v2, Lemmas 3.2–3.4][Montanari], under its positive-temperature support assumption, and in the zero-temperature calculations of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1, Lemmas 6.5 and 6.13][EAMS]. [Sellke, preprint v4, Proposition 3.10 and Lemma 3.11, p. 17][Sellke] gives the closely related finite-cutoff cancellation by applying Itô's formula to $\Phi$ and $x\Phi_x$. ### 5.2 The classical algorithm Full support and existence give an attained, strictly increasing minimiser in the monotone zero-temperature class. This is Assumption 2 of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1][EAMS]. Their Corollary 2.2 then gives, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a randomised algorithm returning a configuration within $\varepsilon n$ of the finite SK maximum with probability tending to one over couplings and algorithmic randomness. Its cost is $C(\varepsilon)n^2$ real-arithmetic operations with the prescribed scalar functions and normalisers available; this includes no separate numerical-preprocessing or finite-precision bound. [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.3][FS] and [long §9.4](../long/reasoning-record.md#classical-algorithm-consequence) check the Gaussian convention and operation count. Chen already records the classical consequence in [§1, p. 4][Chen]. In their incremental approximate message-passing construction, the noise and drift coefficients are, in our notation, $$ u_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=a(t,x),\qquad v_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=\gamma(t)u(t,x). $$ Thus their noise multiplier is the Hessian, whereas our $u$ is the gradient. The bounded martingale $M_t$ and $\mathbb E a^2=1$ give the required variance normalisation. With the fixed-strip regularity and discretisation estimates, [their Theorem 2][EAMS] achieves energy arbitrarily close to the truncated first-moment integral in (10). Strict positivity of the density is unnecessary.
